blocks.text: A potentiometer is mainly used to compare potential differences and to find the value of an unknown resistance. The book says it works on the principle of the Wheatstone bridge: like the bridge, it is used at a balance (null) point.

Potential difference is usually measured by an instrument called a voltmeter, connected across the two points between which the potential difference is to be measured. The resistance of the voltmeter must be large compared with the circuit resistance across which it is connected; otherwise an appreciable current will flow through the voltmeter, altering the circuit current and the potential difference to be measured. Thus a voltmeter reads the correct potential difference only when it draws no current from the circuit; an ideal voltmeter would have an infinite resistance. Some instruments, such as the digital voltmeter and the cathode-ray oscilloscope, practically draw no current because of their large resistance and are very accurate, but they are expensive and difficult to use. A very simple instrument which can measure and compare potential differences accurately is the potentiometer.

A potentiometer consists of a resistor R in the form of a wire on which a terminal C can slide (Fig. 9.31a). The resistance between A and C can be varied from 0 to R as the sliding contact C is moved from A to B. If a battery of emf E is connected across R (Fig. 9.31b), the current through it is I = E/R. If r is the resistance between A and C, the potential drop between these points is rI = rE/R. Thus as C is moved from A to B, r varies from 0 to R and the potential drop between A and C changes from 0 to E. Such an arrangement is also known as a potential divider.

The potential divider can measure the unknown emf of a source (Fig. 9.32). R is in the form of a straight wire of uniform cross-section. The cell whose emf Ex is to be measured is connected between A and the sliding contact C through a galvanometer G; the positive terminal of Ex and that of the potential divider are connected to the same point A. If, in the loop AGCA, the point C and the negative terminal of Ex are at the same potential, the two terminals of the galvanometer are at the same potential and no current flows through it. So the position of C is adjusted until the galvanometer shows no deflection; then the emf Ex equals the potential difference between A and C, whose value Er/R is known. For a wire of uniform cross-section the resistance is proportional to length, so Ex = E r/R = E l/L ... (9.52), where L is the total length of the wire AB and l its length from A to C after C has been adjusted for no deflection.

As the maximum potential that can be obtained between A and C is E, the unknown emf Ex should not exceed this value; otherwise the null condition will not be obtained. The unknown emf is determined when no current is drawn from it, so the potentiometer is one of the most accurate methods of measuring potential.

The same method can compare the emfs E1 and E2 of two cells. The balancing lengths l1 and l2 are found separately for the two cells; then E1 = E l1/L and E2 = E l2/L. Dividing, E1/E2 = l1/l2 ... (9.53). So the ratio of the emfs is equal to the ratio of the balancing lengths.

blocks.prompt: What is a potentiometer? Describe its working (comprehensive question 9.5). Why is it more accurate than an ordinary voltmeter?
blocks.explanation: It is a long uniform resistance wire carrying a steady current from a driver cell, so the potential falls evenly along it; an unknown emf is connected through a galvanometer to a sliding contact, which is moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection, and then Ex = E l/L. At balance it draws no current from the cell being measured, so it measures the true emf, while a voltmeter always draws some current and therefore reads the lower terminal voltage.

items: A voltmeter is accurate only if it draws no current. Potentiometer: uniform wire AB with sliding contact C and driver cell E; potential divider rE/R from 0 to E.
Null method: Ex = E l/L (9.52), Ex must not exceed E; E1/E2 = l1/l2 (9.53); no current is drawn from the unknown cell, so it is very accurate.
